NEGRO LYNCHED.
(BY A) ASSOCIATED PRESS

COUSHANA, La., Aug. 21. An unidentified negro accused of having attempted to attack a young woman was taken from a deputy sheriff near here today. and lynched.
coushatta-coushatta-1915-08-21.A3:
Mob Lynches Negro Who Broke Into Girl's Room
SHREVEPORT, La., Aug. 22.—An unidentified negro who entered the bed room of the seventeen-year-old daughter of Edward Adcock, a planter living near Coushatta, was hanged by a mob in Grand Bayou swamp shortly afterward.

The negro was taken into custody by a sheriff's deputy.
coushatta-coushatta-1915-08-21.A5:
NEGRO ASSAILANT
LYNCHED BY MOB
Fought Off By Girl, He Was Dealt Summarily With Before Of- ficers Arrived.
COUSHAMA, La., Aug. 21.—An unknown negro was lynched by a body of armed men near this place early Saturday morning, following an attempt made by the negro to criminally assault the 17-year-old daughter of Ed Adcock, a well-known farmer.

The young woman, after retiring, discovered the man in her room and after fighting him off gave the alarm. Neighbors caught the black a few minutes afterward and turned him over to a deputy sheriff. Before the officer could get away with his prisoner a mob formed, forced the deputy to give up the negro, and hanged him in a earby swamp.

event.A1: The Williston Courier prints a story about the sheriff of Levy county being seen out in the woods attempting to lynch a couple of negroes. The story should be investigated. If it is true, the sheriff should be dismissed from office. If it is untrue, he should sue the Courier for criminal libel. Its a plain case, cne way or the other.
event.A2: That story in the Williston Courier about the sheriff of Levy county being implicated in a lynching, like most of the stories in that sheet, proves to be a fake. It seems that two negroes living near Raleigh were arrested on a charge of cow stealing and taken to Williston. These negroes say that certain Williston men took them out and threatened to lynch them if they did not confess. They were bound and blindfolded and ropes put around their necks, and, they say, they were hauled off the ground with the ropes and choked two or three times each in the attempt to make them implicate themselves or somebody else. The sheriff says that he took the negroes, by their own consent, out in the woods, with a photographer, and bound them in order to obtain pictures, which he intends to use as evidence against the men who gave them the third degree. He produces affidavits of the men concerned to prove that he tells the truth. The affidavits also affirm that the negroes were treated with extreme cruelty by Williston men.

james-fox-tunnel-springs-1915-08-10.A1:
NEGRO LYNCHED FOR ATTACKING OFFICER
MOBILE, ALA., Aug. 9.—A special to the Item from Tunnel Springs, Ala., says:

A negro named Fox was lynched last night by a mob at the camp of the Alger-Sullivan Lumber Co., eight miles north of this place, after he had shot and dangerously wounded a deputy sheriff, whose name could not be learned here, stationed at the lumber company's camp.

Shortly after the negro's attack upon the deputy the mob gathered and entered upon a successful pursuit of the negro Fox. The negro was then shot and afterward hanged, but reports here state that he was dead before he was strung up.

IMPORTANT NEWS
ITEMS
New York, Aug. 9.—Gen. Benjamin F. Tracy, who was President Harrison's secretary of the navy, died of paralysis here on Friday in his eighty-fifth year after a period of unconsciousness lasting nine days. Three years ago General Tracy sustained a shock of paralysis, but rallied from it after a fey weeks and was able to resume his law practice. He was badly shaken up in an automobile accident last Decoration lay, but from this, too, he speedily recovered.

Chicago, Aug. 9.—Warden E. M. Allen of Jollet penitentiary resigned his position on Friday. The warden sent a telegram to Governor Dunne giving up his place following a receipt of a letter from the governor in which he was informed that the Illinois law requires him to live inside the prison.

Washington, Aug. 10.—George E Downey, comptroller of the treasury, was appointed to the court of claims bench. He was named in place of A. Mitchell Palmer, who resigned.

Mobile, Ala., Aug. 10.—James Fox, a negro, was lynched by a mob at the camp of the Lager Sullivan Lumber company.
